content: In single-dose studies involving patients with nonanuric renal failure, high doses of Demadex (ranging from 20 mg to 200 mg) significantly increased water and sodium excretion. However, in patients with nonanuric renal failure severe enough to require hemodialysis, chronic treatment with up to 200 mg of Demadex daily did not alter steady-state fluid retention. In a study of acute renal failure, patients receiving total daily doses of Demadex ranging from 520 mg to 1200 mg experienced seizures in 19% of cases. Among the 96 patients treated in this study, 6 out of 32 patients treated with torsemide experienced seizures, 6 out of 32 patients treated with comparably high doses of furosemide experienced seizures, and 1 out of 32 patients treated with placebo experienced a seizure. When administered alongside aldosterone antagonists, Demadex also increased sodium and fluid excretion in patients with edema or ascites due to hepatic cirrhosis. The urinary sodium excretion rate relative to the urinary excretion rate of Demadex is lower in cirrhotic patients compared to healthy individuals. This may be attributed to hyperaldosteronism and the resulting sodium retention characteristic of portal hypertension and ascites. However, due to increased renal clearance of Demadex in patients with hepatic cirrhosis, these factors tend to balance each other, resulting in an overall natriuretic response similar to that observed in healthy individuals. Chronic use of any diuretic in hepatic disease has not been studied in adequately controlled trials. In patients with essential hypertension, controlled studies have demonstrated that Demadex effectively lowers blood pressure when administered once daily at doses of 5 mg to 10 mg. The antihypertensive effect is near maximal after 4 to 6 weeks of treatment but may continue to increase for up to 12 weeks. Both systolic and diastolic blood pressures, whether measured in the supine or standing position, are reduced. There is no significant orthostatic effect, and the peak-to-trough difference in blood pressure reduction is minimal. The antihypertensive effects of Demadex, like those of other diuretics, are generally more pronounced in Black patients (a low-renin population) compared to non-Black patients. When Demadex is first administered, daily urinary sodium excretion increases for at least a week. With chronic administration, daily sodium loss equilibrates with dietary sodium intake. If Demadex administration is abruptly discontinued, blood pressure gradually returns to pretreatment levels over several days without overshooting. Demadex has been co-administered with β-adrenergic blocking agents, ACE inhibitors, and calcium-channel blockers. No adverse drug interactions have been observed, and no special dosage adjustments have been necessary. Demadex is available for oral administration as white, scored tablets containing 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, or 100 mg of torsemide. These tablets are supplied in bottles of 100. Each tablet is debossed on the scored side with the Boehringer Mannheim logo and a code (102, 103, 104, or 105 for 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, or 100 mg, respectively). The opposite side of the tablet is debossed with the dose (5, 10, 20, or 100). Storage instructions specify that Demadex should be stored at temperatures between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). Limited information is available regarding the storage of torsemide tablets in the drug label. There is limited information regarding patient counseling for torsemide tablets in the drug label. Additionally, the interaction between alcohol and torsemide has not been established. Patients are advised to consult their doctor about the effects of consuming alcohol while taking this medication.
